title: How to Get an Adult ADHD Assessment in the US
body_markdown:
If you've been wondering whether you might have ADHD, you're far from alone. More and more adults are seeking assessment every year, especially as awareness grows and the shame around late-diagnosed ADHD starts to fade.


But getting an actual ADHD assessment in the US has gotten complicated, and there can be a lot of confusion about who to trust. We hear it constantly from our community: *where do I even start, and how do I know I'll be treated well?*


This guide walks through what a quality ADHD assessment looks like, what to look for in a provider, and how to find one you can trust.


## Why finding the right provider matters


Not all ADHD assessments are created equal. Some providers can turn around a diagnosis in a 15-minute video call. Others take hours, use validated clinical instruments, factor in your full history, and look for other things that can look like ADHD but aren't (anxiety, trauma, sleep issues, thyroid conditions, and more).


A rushed diagnosis can mean:


- Missing a co-occurring condition that needs its own treatment
- Being prescribed medication that isn't right for you
- Getting labelled with something that doesn't actually fit
- Losing access to your prescription if the provider shuts down


A thorough diagnosis gives you a foundation you can build on. It's worth taking the time to get it right.


## What a good ADHD assessment looks like


A quality adult ADHD assessment usually includes:


- **A detailed clinical interview** , typically 45-60 minutes for the first appointment, where a licensed provider walks through your current symptoms and childhood history
- **Validated screening instruments** , like the ASRS, CAARS, or DIVA-5, which have been studied and shown to reliably assess ADHD symptoms
- **Differential diagnosis** , meaning the provider actively considers whether something else might be going on (anxiety, depression,[autism (AuDHD)](https://www.shimmer.care/blog/audhd-autism-adhd-comorbidity) , trauma, sleep disorders)
- **Collateral information when relevant** , like input from a partner, family member, or old report cards that help confirm childhood onset
- **A real treatment plan** , not just a prescription, that discusses medication, behavioral support, lifestyle changes, and follow-up


## How to find an adult ADHD assessment provider


There's no single right path. Depending on your insurance, location, and preferences, a few options worth considering:


- **Check your insurance provider's directory.** Most major insurers have a search tool for in-network psychiatrists who treat ADHD. This is often the fastest way to find care that's covered by your plan
- **Ask your primary care doctor for a referral.** PCPs often know which local psychiatrists are good at adult ADHD, and some insurance plans require a referral anyway
- **Search for ADHD-specialized providers.** Not every psychiatrist is experienced in adult ADHD. Looking for providers who list it as a specialty tends to lead to a better assessment, especially if you're a woman, AFAB, or late-diagnosed
- **Consider national in-network virtual practices.** For folks without a local option or with long wait times, national virtual psychiatry practices can be a strong fit (more on our top pick below)


Whichever route you take, the quality signals above are what to look for: a thorough first appointment, validated instruments, differential diagnosis, and a real plan for ongoing care.


### Questions worth asking any ADHD provider


In the CHADD article, “[Where Can Adults with ADHD Find the Best Treatment?](https://chadd.org/adhd-news/adhd-news-adults/where-can-adults-with-adhd-find-the-best-treatment-2/) ”, Dr. Oren W. Mason suggests two particularly revealing questions to ask any ADHD practice before you book:


1. **How many patients with ADHD do you currently treat?** A good rule of thumb is an active ADHD panel of 50-100+. Enough that the provider is seeing the full range of presentations and keeping up with the research
2. **Do you (or your practice) like treating ADHD?** Not every mental health provider enjoys ADHD care. The answer tells you whether you're walking into a practice that's genuinely interested, or one that treats it as an afterthought


A few practical things worth checking on the practice website or during an intake call:


- Average wait time for a first evaluation
- Insurance accepted and typical out-of-pocket costs
- Standard follow-up cadence (ongoing ADHD care usually means 2-12 visits per year)
- Whether telehealth is available
- Whether the practice offers or refers to ancillary services like therapy, ADHD coaching, or educational specialists


That last one matters more than people realize. The strongest ADHD care is multimodal, as noted above. Practices that acknowledge this, either by offering those services themselves or by actively referring to specialists in them, tend to deliver better outcomes.


*Source: Mason, O.W.,*["Where Can Adults with ADHD Find the Best Treatment?"](https://chadd.org/adhd-news/adhd-news-adults/where-can-adults-with-adhd-find-the-best-treatment-2/) *CHADD Attention Magazine, October 2019.*

## What to expect from the Talkiatry process


Here's a rough walkthrough of what the Talkiatry experience looks like:


1. **Online intake.** You answer a set of screening questions to help match you with the right psychiatrist. You can also book directly via[https://talkiatry.care/shimmer](https://talkiatry.care/shimmer) or call 929-484-2024
2. **Get matched (within days).** Most patients can be seen in less than 7 days
3. **First appointment (60 min).** A full psychiatric evaluation with a licensed psychiatrist, covering current symptoms, history, and goals
4. **Diagnosis and treatment plan.** If ADHD is the diagnosis, you'll discuss medication options (including stimulants, where appropriate) and a plan for ongoing care
5. **Follow-up appointments (typically monthly or every few months).** Ongoing medication management, side effect monitoring, and treatment adjustments, with the same psychiatrist each time for continuity


## How to prepare for your ADHD assessment


Showing up prepared makes a real difference, especially since many first appointments are only 45-60 minutes. The more concrete you can be about your experience, the better your provider can assess what's going on. A few things worth doing before your appointment:


- **Write out your symptoms with specific examples.** Not just "I have trouble focusing" but "I regularly start three projects at work and finish none of them by the deadline" or "I lose my keys multiple times a week." Concrete examples anchor an assessment far better than general descriptions
- **Pull evidence of childhood symptoms.** ADHD is a developmental condition, which means symptoms have to have been present in childhood (even if they weren't recognized). Old report cards, memories of school struggles, or a conversation with a parent or older sibling can all help. Common childhood signals: being called "smart but not applying yourself," struggling to finish homework, chronic lateness, forgetting assignments, trouble sitting still, daydreaming
- **Think about family history.** ADHD has a strong genetic component. Any family members with diagnosed ADHD, learning differences, anxiety, depression, or substance use issues are worth noting
- **List what you've already tried.** Previous medications (ADHD or otherwise), therapy modalities, coaching, lifestyle changes, supplements, and productivity systems. What's worked, what hasn't, and what you're currently on
- **Bring your own questions.** Things like: What assessment instruments will you use? How do you decide between stimulants and non-stimulants? What's your approach if medication isn't the right fit? How often will we meet after diagnosis? What's your referral network for therapy and coaching?


If you're a late-diagnosed adult, especially a woman or AFAB person, it's worth noting any patterns that are specifically associated with less-recognized ADHD presentations: internalized symptoms (anxiety, perfectionism, people-pleasing), masking, chronic burnout, strong academic performance that collapsed in adulthood when structure disappeared. Providers who specialize in adult ADHD will recognize these patterns, but surfacing them explicitly helps.


## What happens after you get diagnosed


Getting the diagnosis is the beginning, not the end. The first six to twelve months after an adult ADHD diagnosis can be a lot, both practically and emotionally. Knowing what to expect helps.


**Finding the right medication and dose.** If you start medication, expect a titration process. Your provider will typically start you on a low dose and adjust based on how you respond, side effects, and how long the medication lasts for you. This usually takes a few months of appointments to dial in. It's normal for the first medication or dose to not be the right one.


**Grief, relief, and anger are all common.** For late-diagnosed adults especially, a diagnosis often brings up a flood of feelings. Relief at finally having an explanation. Grief for the years spent struggling without one. Anger at teachers, parents, or systems that missed it. Reframing your whole life story through an ADHD lens takes time and is often harder than people expect. Totally normal.


**Treatment usually works best as a mix.** Medication can be transformative for focus, impulse control, and energy regulation. Alongside it, behavioral support (coaching, therapy, or both) helps you rebuild the systems, routines, and self-trust that got eroded over years of struggling. Research consistently shows that multimodal treatment produces better long-term outcomes than any one modality alone. Here's how the pieces fit together:


- **Medication** addresses the neurochemistry: attention regulation, impulse control, executive function
- **Therapy** addresses the emotional: the anxiety, shame, trauma, or self-worth stuff that often shows up alongside ADHD, especially for late-diagnosed adults
- **ADHD coaching** addresses the practical: building systems, routines, and strategies that work with your ADHD brain. The place where insight turns into daily change


The three work differently and complement each other.


This is where coaching, therapy, and community become part of the picture.

## FAQs


**I think I might have ADHD but I'm not sure. Should I get assessed?**


If you've been wondering for a while, it's probably worth a conversation. A good assessment either confirms what you suspected or points you toward what else might be going on. Either outcome is useful.


**How much does an adult ADHD assessment cost?**


It depends on the provider and your insurance. If you go in-network with a practice like Talkiatry, most patients pay around $30 out of pocket per visit. If you go out-of-network or self-pay, a full adult ADHD evaluation typically runs $400-$1,500+ depending on the provider and whether it's a psychiatric evaluation or a full neuropsychological battery. A full neuropsych evaluation (6-10+ hours of testing, used for school or workplace accommodations) can run $2,000-$5,000+ out of pocket.


**How long does an adult ADHD assessment take?**


Most standard psychiatric ADHD assessments involve a 45-60 minute first appointment with a clinical interview and validated screening instruments, with a follow-up visit to discuss results and treatment. A full neuropsychological evaluation is longer: typically 6-10+ hours of testing over 1-2 days, plus a written report.


**Can I get an ADHD diagnosis online?**


Yes. Virtual psychiatric practices can diagnose adult ADHD remotely using clinical interviews and validated screening instruments. Virtual providers cannot administer full neuropsychological batteries (those require in-person, specialized testing), so if you need that level of documentation for workplace or school accommodations, you'll want to see an in-person neuropsychologist. For most adults seeking diagnosis and treatment, a virtual psychiatric evaluation is clinically sufficient.


**Does Shimmer coaching require a diagnosis?**


No. Our coaching is subclinical and works for anyone with ADHD traits, whether you're formally diagnosed, self-identifying, or still figuring it out.
